SELinux in Practice

1. SELinux in Practice

HarborWorks moves static web content from a distribution directory to /srv/harbor/site. The files are readable by the web worker, yet requests fail. The correct response is not “SELinux is broken.” The system has a policy describing which types of content the web service may read; the move may have changed the labels that express that intent.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — Chapter 18 — SELinux in Practice

2. Ordinary permissions and SELinux policy

A request must satisfy discretionary access and the applicable SELinux policy. Persistent file-context intent differs from a temporary label edit. chmod 777 is applied to a type-enforcement denial and the request still fails.

SOURCE: Ordinary permissions and SELinux policy

3. Chapter 18 — SELinux in Practice

HarborWorks moves static web content from a distribution directory to /srv/harbor/site. The files are readable by the web worker, yet requests fail. SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — Chapter 18 — SELinux in Practice

4. 18.1 Why SELinux Exists

Ordinary permissions answer whether a user or group may access an object. A compromised service still acts with its assigned identity, so every file readable by that identity can become part of the attack surface. SELinux can impose an additional policy boundary on the service’s domain.

The benefit depends on keeping the policy meaningful. Giving a web service broad access to arbitrary files simply because a deployment chose a convenient location undermines the boundary. Prefer a dedicated content path and an appropriate existing type for the required operation. (R39)

Linux example — 18.1

Inspect whether SELinux is active.

What to check: If tools or policy are absent, use the host's actual mandatory-access-control system.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.1 Why SELinux Exists

6. 18.2 Mandatory Access Control

Mandatory access control means the policy is enforced independently of a file owner’s ordinary discretionary permission choices. A user cannot necessarily make a file accessible to a confined service merely by running chmod 777.

Access normally must satisfy all relevant layers: path traversal, Unix mode or ACL rules, mount properties, SELinux policy, and possibly service sandboxing. A denial at any one can stop the operation. This layered model explains why fixing a Unix group can leave an SELinux problem unchanged and vice versa.

Linux example — 18.2

Compare credentials, file modes, and SELinux context.

What to check: A discretionary permission grant does not override a mandatory policy denial.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.2 Mandatory Access Control

8. 18.3 Users, Roles, Types, and Levels

A context often appears as user:role:type:level. SELinux users are not simply the same namespace as Linux login names. Roles organize permitted transitions, types classify objects and process domains, and levels support additional separation such as MLS or MCS configurations.

On the targeted RHEL teaching policy, type enforcement is the main focus for ordinary service troubleshooting. Do not generalize every teaching type or transition to an MLS deployment or custom enterprise policy. Read the active policy and the installed service-specific manual when behavior differs.

Linux example — 18.3

Display a process's full SELinux context.

What to check: Context fields represent user, role, type, and level; interpret them under the installed policy.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.3 Users, Roles, Types, and Levels

10. 18.4 Security Contexts

Use ls -Zd /srv/harbor/site for a directory’s context and ls -Z /srv/harbor/site for its contents. The -d option prevents ls from listing inside the directory when the directory itself is the object under inspection.

A file’s current context and its policy-defined expected context are different observations. Tools such as matchpathcon can show the expected mapping where available. A copied file may inherit a destination label; a moved file may retain its old label. File movement therefore deserves a label check during deployment.

Linux example — 18.4

Inspect directory and file labels.

What to check: The object type helps determine allowed domain-to-object operations.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.4 Security Contexts

12. 18.5 Type Enforcement

Type enforcement governs which process domains may perform which operations on object types. Static content conventionally uses a readable web-content type such as httpd_sys_content_t in the RHEL targeted policy. Writable application content may need a different narrowly scoped type.

Do not relabel the entire application tree writable because one cache directory needs writes. Separate immutable code, static content, uploads, runtime state, and secrets into deliberate paths. This makes both Unix permissions and SELinux policy easier to express and audit.

Linux example — 18.5

Observe domains of running processes.

What to check: Type-enforcement decisions depend on the source domain, target type, class, and operation.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.5 Type Enforcement

14. 18.6 SELinux Booleans

Booleans enable predefined policy variations. Inspect with getsebool and, when installed, semanage boolean -l. A Boolean can permit a class of behavior, such as a web domain initiating certain network connections, without writing a custom module.

Its scope may be broader than one process or destination. Read the description and service documentation before changing it. setsebool -P makes a change persistent; a runtime-only change does not survive policy reload or reboot in the same way. Record the previous value and why the changed behavior is required.

Linux example — 18.6

Inspect a web-related Boolean without changing it.

What to check: A disabled Boolean may be the intended policy; enable only the permission the workload actually requires.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.6 SELinux Booleans

16. 18.7 getenforce and setenforce

getenforce reports the current enforcement mode. setenforce changes between enforcing and permissive at runtime where SELinux is enabled. It does not turn a disabled system into a fully enabled and correctly labeled one.

Permissive mode can be a controlled diagnostic tool, but globally removing enforcement is not the normal repair. A real service failure needs an explanation of the attempted operation and the correct policy relationship. A test that works only with enforcement removed has identified a layer, not completed the fix.

Linux example — 18.7

Read enforcement state and the mode-changing tool's help.

What to check: Do not change the mode for a routine label problem; diagnosis should preserve enforcement.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.7 getenforce and setenforce

18. 18.8 ls -Z

The -Z option displays contexts alongside directory entries. Combine it with ordinary owner and mode inspection rather than replacing those observations. For example, ls -ldZ /srv/harbor /srv/harbor/site reveals permissions and contexts at two traversal points.

Avoid assuming that the leaf file is the only relevant object. A service can be denied searching a parent directory before it ever attempts to read the page. Follow the complete path, then compare it with the operation named in the denial record.

Linux example — 18.8

Show labels with long file metadata.

What to check: The context is additional evidence beyond owner, group, and mode.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.8 ls -Z

20. 18.9 restorecon

restorecon applies expected labels according to configured file-context mappings. Use a dry-run form such as restorecon -nRv PATH to inspect proposed changes before applying a recursive relabel in a bounded application tree.

restorecon -Rv PATH does not invent the appropriate custom mapping. If /srv/harbor/site has not been assigned the intended persistent type, restoring its default may preserve the wrong result for the application. Establish the mapping first, then apply it, and inspect the outcome. (R39)

Linux example — 18.9

Preview expected-label restoration.

What to check: -n reports proposed changes without applying them; ensure the persistent mapping is correct first.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.9 restorecon

22. 18.10 semanage

semanage manages persistent SELinux policy configuration such as file-context mappings and port labels. On RHEL-family systems the command is commonly provided by policycoreutils-python-utils. Install supported packages rather than downloading random helper scripts.

A dedicated static-content mapping can be added with semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/harbor/site(/.*)?' when no conflicting local mapping exists. The quoted expression matches the directory and descendants. If a mapping already exists, inspect it and deliberately modify the intended entry rather than repeatedly trying to add duplicates.

Linux example — 18.10

List local file-context customizations.

What to check: Local rules can override defaults; inspect before adding or modifying a mapping.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.10 semanage

24. 18.11 Diagnosing AVC Denials

AVC denial records describe denied access decisions. Look for source context, target context, object class, requested permission, process information, and the relevant path or object. A denial of name_connect is a different problem from a denial of read on a file.

Reproduce one authorized request in a narrow time window, then inspect the corresponding records. Old unrelated denials can lead to the wrong fix. Absence of a visible denial is not proof SELinux is irrelevant: audit access, retention, suppression, and earlier failing permission layers may affect what you see.

Linux example — 18.11

Find recent access denials.

What to check: Correlate source domain, target label, operation, and application time before proposing a fix.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.11 Diagnosing AVC Denials

26. 18.12 ausearch

ausearch queries audit records. A common bounded investigation begins with sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC -ts recent, followed by a more specific time or process filter as needed. Read the grouped event rather than extracting one token out of context.

Do not pipe every denial directly into an automatic policy generator and install the result. A generated allow rule can formalize an attack or a misconfiguration as permitted behavior. First check documented labels, port types, booleans, and intended paths; create custom policy only when the required behavior is legitimate and existing policy interfaces do not express it.

Linux example — 18.12

Query recent audit records for SSH.

What to check: An empty result may reflect no matching event, retention, or audit configuration.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.12 ausearch

28. 18.13 Solving Real SELinux Problems

Classify the resource. For wrong file labels, use a persistent mapping and restorecon. For a legitimate nonstandard listening port, inspect the policy’s existing port mapping and assign an appropriate type without stealing a port already classified for another service. For an approved optional behavior, examine the relevant Boolean.

After the smallest correction, repeat the original application request with enforcement active. Check that intended access succeeds and that unrelated protected resources remain inaccessible. Document the exact mapping or policy change so a rebuild reproduces the result.

Linux example — 18.13

Compare actual and expected labels on the capstone site.

What to check: Requires the Chapter 18 lab site; apply a narrowly reviewed persistent mapping if expectations are wrong.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.13 Solving Real SELinux Problems

30. 18.14 Why Disabling SELinux Is Usually the Wrong Fix

Disabling SELinux removes a boundary from the whole host and conceals the mismatch that caused the failure. It also turns future troubleshooting into a different environment from the supported baseline. The service may appear repaired while its access becomes broader than intended.

A correct fix teaches you something precise: this domain needed read access to this dedicated content type, or this documented network behavior needed an approved Boolean. Keep that explanation in the deployment configuration. An exception, when genuinely required, should be scoped, approved, monitored, and temporary where possible.

Linux example — 18.14

Preserve enforcement while gathering denial evidence.

What to check: Disabling policy removes a protection layer and conceals the original cause rather than correcting it.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — 18.14 Why Disabling SELinux Is Usually the Wrong Fix

32. Requirement and preconditions

On the enforcing RHEL 9-family lab VM, NGINX will read static files from /srv/harbor/site. The directory is newly created for this lab, contains no secrets or unrelated data, and no existing local SELinux mapping covers it with a conflicting intent. NGINX setup and the application request are completed in Chapter 19.

Create the dedicated tree and a harmless page with conventional traversal and read permissions. Inspect both ordinary and mandatory access-control state:

The simplest shortcut would be chcon on one file. Its limitation is that it does not express a durable path mapping and can be undone by a later relabel.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — Requirement and preconditions

34. Persistent correction

After reviewing existing mappings:

If the add operation says the mapping already exists, stop and inspect it; do not silently delete an unknown rule. The dry run exposes the planned label changes. The actual relabel should affect only this dedicated content tree.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — Persistent correction

37. Verification and recovery

Once NGINX serves this path, perform the exact HTTP request and inspect recent AVC records. Enforcing mode must remain active. Successful ls by an administrator is not the service test.

For lab removal, stop using the content tree, remove only the exact local mapping you added with semanage fcontext -d using the same expression, and restore default labels if the directory remains. Do not delete all local mappings. A production rollback should restore the prior known mapping and application release together.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — Verification and recovery

38. Practice and implementation lab

Compare the context on a file copied into the content directory with one moved from a differently labeled lab location. Inspect before and after restorecon. Explain the difference between a current label, a persistent mapping, and a policy allow rule.

Check your understanding. Does chmod 777 bypass SELinux? No. Does restorecon know your application intent without an appropriate mapping? No. Is an automatically generated allow rule necessarily safe? No.

Chapter takeaway. SELinux troubleshooting succeeds when intended behavior, persistent labeling, and the actual service request agree under enforcement.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch020.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

39. Separate discretionary and type-enforcement decisions

A type-policy model explains an independent boundary. It neither invokes nor tests a real SELinux policy. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Separate discretionary and type-enforcement decisions
